newsitem.title: RUSSIA: EU chiefs in Moscow as Yeltsin starts testing week.
newsitem.headline: EU chiefs in Moscow as Yeltsin starts testing week.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin meets European Union leaders on Monday at the start of a week which will test his strength after his long absences from the Kremlin because of illness.
During the week Yeltsin, 66, is expected to work on a cabinet reshuffle, give a keynote speech to parliament and have talks with Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko.
He starts by holding wide-ranging talks with EU Commission President Jacques Santer and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, whose country holds the EU's rotating presidency.

The pair met Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday morning. Interfax news agency quoted him as telling them their talks with Yeltsin would give a "powerful new boost" to Moscow's relations with the EU.
He hoped for progress on a still unratified accord designed to forge links between the two sides and liberalise trade.

The EU leaders are likely to back Moscow's political and economic reforms and urge Yeltsin to prepare Russia fully for membership of the World Trade Organisation. Other likely topics include organised crime and the fight against illegal drugs.

The prospect that some of Russia's former communist allies in eastern and central Europe will eventually join the EU causes much less concern in Moscow than the planned eastward expansion of NATO, which Russia says threatens its security.
Aides to NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana are expected in Moscow on Tuesday ahead of Solana's visit next weekend to continue the search for a deal to ease Russia's concerns.
Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov briefed Yeltsin on Sunday on his latest talks with NATO member states. "Talks made progress in several areas," the presidential press office said.
But it made clear major differences with NATO remained.
Yeltsin got some comfort when Russian and Chechen negotiators said they hoped a political agreement, amounting to a formal peace treaty, would be signed in the next eight days.

Even so, the two sides did not alter their stances on Chechnya's independence demands which prompted a 21-month conflict. Russia still rules out secession, while leaders of the rebel region say it is already independent.
Yeltsin, who is under pressure from opponents to quit for health reasons, faces his biggest test of the week when he gives an annual policy address to parliament on Thursday.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would speak for 40 minutes -- the longest he has stood in public since he had heart problems just before being re-elected last July.
Yeltsin has signalled he will announce a cabinet reshuffle, after criticism of the government's failure to pay wages and pensions. He has not said when the reshuffle will be.

Valentin Kuptsov, a deputy leader of the Communist party, told a meeting of the party's Central Committee on Monday that patience with the government was running out and it could face a no-confidence motion next month in the opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament.
Kuptsov said Chernomyrdin had failed to meet communist demands to pay out wage and pension arrears as he had promised to do in order to secure the party's backing for the government's 1997 budget.
"There could be an expression of no confidence in the government if these conditions are not met by March 31 or concrete measures to fulfil them are not presented," he said.
Under Russia's constitution, parliament has little practical power to oust the government appointed by the president.
